card vi-board  [decided]
A ticket board is a view beside the map, the graph, and the diagram
why: Tickets are units of build work, not decisions. A person reads them as columns to move through, not as a tree.
subtree: 5 cards, 5 decided, 1 unchallenged

A small board in the style of Trello. One column per ticket state, one card per ticket (#st-ticket). It follows the tickets through the whole run.

On the board, a ticket card shows only its title. Clicking a card opens a drawer beneath the board: the slice (often a few hundred words, since a real ticket brief is long) sits in a main column on the left, and the metadata and relations — the map cards it cites, what blocks it, retries, files, checks (#st-ticket's fields) — sit in a sidebar on the right. A click on a cited id in the sidebar opens that card on the map. A ticket that has retried more than once shows a small retry count next to its title.

A ticket with unmet blocked_by tickets shows a small count next to its title too, one per not-done ticket it depends on — the same kind of blocking-issue count Linear shows.

A building ticket with a live agent session pulses. It stops the moment the session ends, whether that is a pass, a failed retry waiting on the next attempt, or a person stopping the build by hand — pulsing means a session is running right now, not just that the ticket sits in building.

For a ticket currently in building, the drawer also shows a live preview of the agent's log, above the slice, in a fixed-height scrolling viewport. Moving out of building — forward or back to ready — drops the preview; it is a window onto a running session, not a permanent transcript.

The columns are in #werk-board-columns. What a person can do on the board is in #werk-board-control.

Settled by iterating on the running app, not by discussion — three rounds of feedback on the
same build:

1. Placement: the strip is its own row, last in the pane — the chat log, the dead-child bar, the asks,
   the chat header row (state · context pie · model select), the composer, then the tab strip. The
   model/context/state row sits above the composer, not attached to the tabs.
2. Shape: a chip is a real tab, not a button. The strip carries one shared top border; the
   active chip erases its own piece of that line by matching the pane's background (`#11161d`,
   the same color the composer above it already shows through to), so it reads as attached to
   whatever is above rather than floating below it. An inactive chip keeps a full border and a
   lighter panel fill so it visibly sits apart until clicked.
3. Edge-to-edge: no horizontal padding on the strip. Tabs start flush at the pane's left edge,
   the way a browser's own tab strip does, instead of sitting indented inside a margin.

Marks, the same in the title, the why line, and the body: added text has a blue highlight. Removed text has a blue highlight and a strikethrough. No `+` in front, no "before" or "after" label. A list or heading is marked line by line. A block that changes shape shows the old block removed and the new block added.

Two kinds of proposal look different:

- **A completely new card**: blue border and blue background. The whole card is the proposal.
- **An edit to an existing card**: blue border only. The changes show as blue inline markers in the text.

Accept and discard are #al-diff-cli and #al-diff-cli-btn.

I tested a copy of the real log on a second server with no errors:

- **Tiles:** counts for cards, open, proto, decided, stale, paused, proposed, and the median time to decide. A click on the stale, paused or proposed tile sets that filter on the list.

- **Subtrees:** a table with a status bar and counts for each subtree. A click on a row limits the whole tab to that subtree. A toggle switches between "direct children" and "every parent", so you can try both answers to the open question.
